questions.q: According to this lesson, why can't a real architecture optimize all five Well-Architected pillars at once?
options: Every design decision draws on the same shared, finite budget of money, operational complexity, and acceptable risk, and the pillars compete for that budget
The pillars were never meant to be used together in the same review
Only Azure workloads face this limitation; AWS workloads do not
Well-Architected tools only allow scoring one pillar per assessment
questions.explain: The pillars are competing claims on the same finite budget of cost, complexity, and risk — improving one measurably can worsen another.

questions.q: In the worked reliability-vs-cost example, what happens when active-active failover is added to the order-processing API?
options: Compute spend stays flat because the secondary region only runs during an actual outage
Reliability improves, but compute cost roughly doubles and operational complexity increases, moving the cost optimization pillar in the opposite direction
Cost optimization improves alongside reliability with no added operational work
Only the security pillar is affected, not cost or reliability
questions.explain: Active-active failover closes the reliability gap but roughly doubles steady-state compute cost and adds operational complexity — a direct tradeoff against cost optimization.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say an untested failover runbook is 'not meaningfully different from no failover path'?
options: Because failover runbooks are purely a documentation exercise with no real function
Because an untested procedure can't be trusted to actually work when the real failure happens, so the reliability benefit it's supposed to provide isn't verified
Because failover only matters for security compliance, not reliability
Because Terraform cannot provision a secondary region without a tested runbook
questions.explain: A failover path that has never been exercised carries real uncertainty about whether it will actually work under a real failure, undermining the reliability gain it's meant to deliver.

questions.q: What question does the lesson say a mature design review should ask explicitly, instead of presenting a fix like multi-region failover as a cost-free win?
options: Whether the fix can be implemented using Bicep instead of Terraform
Whether the fix will pass a Well-Architected assessment tool's automated score
Whether this specific workload's revenue-per-minute of downtime justifies the added cost and operational commitment the fix requires
Whether the fix increases the number of Kubernetes pods running
questions.explain: The lesson frames the real question as weighing the specific cost and operational commitment of a fix against what failure actually costs that specific business.

questions.q: Why might an internal reporting dashboard used twice a month legitimately choose cost optimization over reliability, according to the lesson?
options: Because cost optimization always outranks reliability for every workload
Because reporting dashboards cannot be deployed with Terraform
Because the Well-Architected Framework exempts internal tools from the reliability pillar entirely

Because its low usage and low business impact mean its cost-optimization claim on the shared budget can reasonably outweigh its reliability claim — a documented, legitimate decision rather than a default
questions.explain: The lesson frames which pillar 'wins' as a business decision made visible through architecture — a low-impact, infrequently used workload can legitimately deprioritize reliability in favor of cost, as long as it's a documented choice.
